tweet.text:
Our agent fine-tuned @NVIDIAAI Nemotron 3.5 Lightning on medical and financial tasks.

It autonomously discovered the best post-training recipes by coming up with some combinations that we never would have thought of. 

Here are the 10 best recipes we’d reuse to fine-tune Lightning 🧵

---

Recipe A (Healthcare)
Healthcare adapter -> 11,776 rows across PubMedQA, MedCalc, HealthBench conversations, and small capped specialist components. Caps were the key. Flooding NER or error-detection data killed conversational skills. More HealthBench data wasn't monotonically better. Rank 32, 8e-5, 2 epochs. The sophistication was in the mixture, not the optimizer.

---

Recipe B (FinQA)
FinQA -> pure program translation, no teacher model needed. 6,251 gold-program targets. A 1,500-row smoke test jumped execution accuracy from ~16% to 68%. Templated explanations lost. Chain-of-thought lost. ConvFinQA conversations hurt. Rule -> when the product is an executable object, spend supervision on the object.

---

Recipe C (TAT-QA)
TAT-QA -> deterministic five-field scaffold (question type, evidence, equation, answer, scale). 13,180 verified rows. Rank 16 tied rank 64. Epochs were the meaningful lever, not adapter size. The scaffold avoided teacher noise entirely and made every training row testable before training began.

---

Recipe D (UNER)
Multilingual NER -> 17,999 examples across 23 languages. 45% were zero-entity or hard negatives, critical for stopping the model from hallucinating entities. Language balancing added ~4.5 F1. Adding one explanatory sentence before structured output cost ~22 F1. The model learned the schema fast once you stopped asking it to do two things at once.

---

Recipe E (GSMPlus)
Math fine-tuning initially failed. Teacher answers were too short and taught terseness, not reasoning. The fix -> self-distillation. Filter the model's own correct solutions, anchor with official-format examples. 8,663 rows, ~11.6 min on 4×H200s. Treat the base model as a source of behavior worth preserving. The teacher's job is selection, not generation.

---

Recipe F (Finance Combined)
Six finance specialists in one adapter (13,698 rows). Mixture was deliberately disproportionate, not scaled by available data. A 449-row tool-use component was repeated twice to protect a fragile behavior that otherwise vanished. Template -> start with proven specialists, cap dominant sources, give fragile skills enough weight to survive.

---

Recipe G (MEDEC)
Medical error detection -> base model was too conservative, defaulting to "no error." 3,258 rows combining physician-style reasoning with extra no-error coverage. Unusually, this task needed 5 epochs at 8e-5. The lesson isn't "train longer." It's that detecting subtle errors and producing corrections takes longer to settle than learning a clean schema.

---

Recipe H (Legal)
Clearest low-data win. 1,369 real rows moved macro F1 from 60.26% to 72.82%. A generic-only control with zero LegalBench templates hit ~73% because it matched the task's structure. 2,281 narrow CUAD rows did worse than 416 mostly-real rows. The model didn't need "more legal data." It needed demonstrations of the right reading and decision interface.

---

Recipe I (BFCL)
Function calling -> 27,542 real trajectories moved overall from 48% to 71.18%. But single-turn rose from 51% to 82% while multi-turn barely moved. The adapter learned tool syntax and schema compliance, not conversational state tracking. Rather than hiding that gap in a strong average, use it to design the next curriculum.

---

Recipe J (CRUXEval)
Code reasoning -> 3,303 rows moved combined score from 76.6% to 81.4%. But input prediction gained 10.4 points while output prediction dropped 0.8. The adapter learned a useful new direction without fully protecting the old one. For bidirectional tasks, monitor each direction as its own specialist inside the combined adapter.
